protections: A secret typed at an interactive prompt is read with echo disabled: Display.prompt(private=True) routes to getpass (lib/ansible/utils/display.py:297-308) and the vault prompts use that branch (lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py:327-333); every caller that forgets private=True falls back to the echoing input() path (lib/ansible/utils/display.py:308).

A secret prompt is only attempted when an interactive terminal is really available: Display.do_var_prompt gates on an isatty test (lib/ansible/utils/display.py:310-335) and build_vault_ids carries the rule that prompt secrets must not be added without a tty (lib/ansible/cli/__init__.py:149-155); the vault and CLI password prompts themselves have no such test.

The stored become password is only released in answer to a prompt that carries a per-invocation random key, so a process on the target cannot forge the prompt: sudo (lib/ansible/plugins/become/sudo.py:93-98) and dzdo (lib/ansible/plugins/become/dzdo.py:89-91) embed self._id, generated per command by _gen_id (lib/ansible/plugins/become/__init__.py:17-19,58-61).

Prompt/answer traffic is kept out of the persistent log: _log_messages is gated on the opt-in persistent_log_messages option and the operator is warned that the log will not redact sensitive configuration such as passwords (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py:341-348,379-381; lib/ansible/plugins/connection/network_cli.py:178-186).

traps.what: ansible-vault encrypt_string --prompt reads the value that is about to be encrypted through the non-private branch of Display.prompt (input()), so the secret is echoed to the terminal while it is typed; the value is then turned into bytes and encrypted with no confirm step, and the neighbouring variable-name prompt uses the same public branch.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: The in-code note says private=True is only 'useful' for shadowed input (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:302), so the echoing prompt reads as an accepted UX choice, and 'String to encrypt' is not a login password; making it private also removes the only way a user can see what they are encrypting.

traps.what: Vault password prompting adds a prompt secret whenever --ask-vault-pass (or create_new_password) is requested and then calls display.prompt(..., private=True) with no test that a terminal exists; when /dev/tty cannot be opened Python getpass falls back to the invoking stdin and warns that input may be echoed, so the password can be echoed and captured, even though the code comment states prompts must not be added without a tty.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: getpass is the canonical hidden-input primitive, so the vault prompt looks protected; the documented remedy for automation is --vault-password-file, and the fallback only matters when no controlling terminal can be opened.

traps.what: CLI connection and become passwords are read by a second, separate prompt implementation: CLI.ask_passwords calls getpass.getpass directly, bypassing Display.prompt and its private parameter, and makes no terminal test either, so the same non-tty stdin fallback applies to the SSH and become prompts reached through adhoc, playbook and console.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: getpass.getpass already turns echo off, so this looks like the safe path, and -k/-K are the most obvious 'password prompt' options a report would name first, so the route looks already handled.

traps.what: ansible-galaxy login is a third prompt implementation: the GitHub username is read with the echoing input() and the GitHub password with a bare getpass.getpass, both outside Display.prompt and without any terminal test, and the credentials are then used for HTTP basic auth.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: The tool tells the user that the password will not be displayed (lib/ansible/galaxy/login.py:57) and getpass does hide it, and ansible-galaxy login is an old, rarely used flow pointed at api.github.com rather than at a managed host.

traps.what: Display.do_var_prompt decides whether it may prompt by testing sys.__stdin__.isatty(), a different object from the stream the value is then read from (getpass opens /dev/tty, input() reads sys.stdin); when a wrapper replaces sys.stdin the guard describes the interpreter's original stdin rather than the stream that will carry the secret, and the prompt/read pair disagree.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: In a normal command-line run sys.stdin is sys.__stdin__, so the guard looks equivalent, and vars_prompt already refuses to prompt when stdin is not interactive (lib/ansible/utils/display.py:333-335).

traps.what: The value sent in answer to a matched device prompt is written to the Ansible log by network_cli._log_messages, and the raw JSON-RPC request/response carrying the same answer is written by ansible-connection; the only protection is the opt-in persistent_log_messages switch plus a warning that the log will not redact passwords.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: Persistent connection logging is off by default, the operator is warned twice that it logs everything and will not redact passwords (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/network_cli.py:184-185, lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py:344-348), and the answer is playbook-supplied configuration rather than a password the user types.

traps.what: Become-prompt detection is reimplemented per become plugin and only sudo and dzdo put a per-invocation random key into the prompt; su, doas, ksu, pbrun, pmrun and sesu match guessable literal or localized prompt text, and every connection plugin releases the stored become password as soon as that text matches, so output the target side can emit before or during escalation can elicit the password.
traps.reason_to_dismiss: The sudo prompt already carries a random key and dzdo copies the pattern, so the mechanism looks solved; the connections only examine output during escalation negotiation before task data is sent (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/ssh.py:928-937), so forging a prompt looks impossible, and su/doas/ksu prompt text is fixed by the localised login program.

masking: T6 only becomes visible once T2/T3/T5 are addressed: while a prompt can still fall back to a non-tty stdin the prompt itself is the louder leak, and after the read is made private the prompt answer already written to the persistent log is the remaining exposure of the same secret.

T1 only becomes visible once T2/T5 are fixed: a terminal test inside Display.prompt stops the non-tty fallback but leaves the encrypt_string call echoing on a real terminal, because that call never asks for private input (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:303).

T7 is only reachable after the connection plugin actually has a stored become password and expects a prompt (lib/ansible/plugins/become/__init__.py:42-46); fixing T3 so the password is collected safely does not stop the password from being released to a forged prompt.

conflicts.what: The blunt fix for T1 (make every Display.prompt private, or change its default) hides the prompts that must stay visible: the variable-name prompt (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:294), the --step prompt (lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/__init__.py:962-966) and pause input (lib/ansible/plugins/action/pause.py:160-163,240-242); the fix has to be per call site.

Requiring a terminal before any secret prompt (the natural T2/T5 fix) also covers the ask_passwords route only if that route is moved onto the same helper; leaving getpass.getpass in place (lib/ansible/cli/__init__.py:263,271) keeps the fallback, while moving it changes the stream the prompt is written to that older Towers match on (lib/ansible/cli/__init__.py:187-188,204-206).

Redacting the prompt answer (T6) removes exactly the data persistent_log_messages is documented to record for device troubleshooting (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/network_cli.py:180-186), so the two fixes pull in opposite directions on the same log.

Requiring an unguessable key in every become prompt cannot be done for su, doas and ksu through their own prompt options: su and doas expose prompt_l10n (lib/ansible/plugins/become/su.py:70-81, lib/ansible/plugins/become/doas.py:69-80) and a nonce would break those localised matchers, so a solver who hardens T3 by refusing prompts without a key disables those become methods.

fairness_risks: A rule that every secret prompt must be hidden contradicts the legitimate use of encrypt_string --prompt to type a long non-secret string and see what is being encrypted; that path has no confirm step (lib/ansible/cli/vault.py:303-309).

A rule that Ansible must never prompt without a tty refuses the piped-stdin automation shapes the vault integration tests rely on (test/integration/targets/vault/runme.sh:328-330) and the setsid prompt simulation at test/integration/targets/vault/runme.sh:353, and it would break ansible-pull/cron style runs that rely on the getpass fallback.

A rule that prompt answers must never reach the log contradicts the documented contract of persistent_log_messages, which is sold as logging every interaction without redaction (lib/ansible/plugins/connection/network_cli.py:180-186, lib/ansible/plugins/connection/__init__.py:344-348).

A rule that become prompts must carry an unguessable key cannot be satisfied for su/doas/ksu, whose prompt text is fixed by the localised login program (lib/ansible/plugins/become/su.py:98-141, lib/ansible/plugins/become/doas.py:102, lib/ansible/plugins/become/ksu.py:101); refusing to answer would disable those become methods entirely.

vars_prompt with private: no is a legitimate documented use (visible input, lib/ansible/executor/playbook_executor.py:126, lib/ansible/utils/display.py:310-332); a blanket rule that all vars_prompt input is hidden would refuse it.

Changing where getpass writes its prompt (routing ask_passwords through Display.prompt) changes the stream and text downstream supervisors match; the vault prompt format is pinned for Tower compatibility (lib/ansible/cli/__init__.py:187-188,204-206) and the SSH/become prompt strings are asserted by tests (test/units/parsing/vault/test_vault.py:140-147).

design.why: Five independent fix sites with five different reasons to dismiss: T1 is a secret prompt that was never made private and is defended by an in-code 'could use private=True if useful' note (deepseek-type absent protection with a dismissal); T2 is the same class in the vault prompt path, defended by the belief that getpass alone is enough even when no tty exists; T3 is a second prompt implementation (raw getpass) that a report points at first and that looks safe; T6 is the log route where the answer to a password prompt is written to the persistent log behind an opt-in warning (deepseek-type producer off the checked path); T7 is the how-type mechanism where only sudo/dzdo authenticate their prompt with a random key while the other become plugins match guessable text (mimo-type deep mechanism, also the only trap matching CWE-287). Because T2 and T5 are closed by one guard inside Display.prompt, T5 is not counted as independent; the five chosen traps need five different edits (the vault.py prompt call, a shared prompt guard, ask_passwords, log redaction, per-plugin prompt keys), so implementing the obvious one (make the vault prompt private, or add a tty check) leaves the others open. The design includes the advisory's own route (T1/T2 prompt reading) and two sibling routes (log, become prompt) that a solver who only edits Display.prompt never reaches.
